papers.title: A Well-Separated Pair Decomposition of Linear Size for Unit-Disk Graphs
papers.abstract: We prove that every connected Euclidean-weighted unit-disk graph on $n$ vertices has a $(1/\varepsilon)$-well-separated pair decomposition of size $O(n\varepsilon^{-2}\log(1/\varepsilon))$. This resolves an open problem posed by Gao and Zhang in 2003. We also show that this bound is tight: there are connected unit-disk graphs for which any $(1/\varepsilon)$-well-separated pair decomposition has size $\Omega(n\varepsilon^{-2}\log (1/\varepsilon))$.

papers.title: Inapproximability of Euclidean Steiner Tree
papers.abstract: We consider the Euclidean Steiner Tree problem of connecting $n$ given points in $\mathbb{R}^d$ by a shortest network allowing the addition of Steiner points anywhere in the space. Arora [FOCS'96/'97, J. ACM'98] gave a polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) for Euclidean Steiner Tree and TSP in every fixed dimension, and Trevisan [STOC'97, SICOMP'00] proved that Euclidean TSP is APX-hard in $O(\log n)$ dimensions. They left open whether Euclidean Steiner Tree admits a PTAS in high dimension. Our first contribution settles this thirty-year-old question by proving APX-hardness in $O(\log n)$ dimensions. Assuming that not all problems in NP can be solved in subexponential time (NP $\not\subseteq $SUBEXP), we also rule out a PTAS for Euclidean Steiner Tree in $O(\log\log n)$ dimensions. This dimension bound is tight up to a factor of $O(\log\log\log n)$, since Arora's scheme is a PTAS in up to $\log\log n/\log\log\log n$ dimensions. In fixed dimension, Kisfaludi-Bak, Nederlof, and W\k{e}grzycki [FOCS'21, J. ACM'25] obtained approximation schemes running in time $2^{O_d(\varepsilon^{-(d-1)})}n\log n$ and proved matching Gap-ETH lower bounds for Euclidean TSP and Rectilinear Steiner Tree, but left a corresponding lower bound for Euclidean Steiner Tree as an open question. Our second contribution answers this question with a nearly tight lower bound on the dependence on accuracy for Euclidean Steiner Tree. However, given the recent claimed refutations of ETH and hence Gap-ETH by OpenAI and Anthropic, we use the weaker assumption that 3SAT has no truly subexponential-time algorithm, that is, no $2^{n^\gamma}$-time algorithm on formulas of size $n$ for any constant $\gamma<1$ (a hypothesis one might call weak ETH). Under this assumption, we prove that no $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm runs in time $2^{O(\varepsilon^{-\gamma(d-1)})} poly(n)$ for any such $\gamma$.

papers.title: Near-Optimal Centerpoints in Polynomial Time in the Ambient Dimension
papers.abstract: An $\alpha$-centerpoint of a set of $n$ input points is a point such that any halfspace containing it contains an $\alpha$-fraction of the input. The first algorithm for centerpoints given by Clarkson, Eppstein, Miller, Sturtivant and Teng [IJCGA, 1996], the best quality centerpoint obtainable in polynomial time in $d$ has been $\Omega(d^{-2})$; computing centerpoints of quality $\Omega(d^{-1})$ required time $d^{\Omega(d)}$. Recently Cherapanamjeri [FOCS, 2024] gave the first polynomial time randomized algorithm for computing \emph{approximate} $\Omega(1/d)$-centerpoints, although the degree of the polynomial as well as associated constants, are large. We give a $\tilde{O}(d^5)$ time randomized algorithm for computing exact $\Omega(1/(d\cdot\ln d\cdot\ln\ln d))$-centerpoints, improving significantly on the long-standing $\Omega(1/d^2)$ quality bound of Clarkson et al. For low-dimensional point-sets, we also give the first algorithm with complexity subexponential in $d$, and independent of the bit-complexity, which achieves a $\omega\pth{d^{-2}}$ quality of the centerpoint, improving on the previous $O(d^d)$ bound. For the Word RAM model, as well as for practical implementations, we also discuss a truncate-and-proceed approach to address bit-size complexity issues. On the way we also get a simple algorithm to compute $O(\sqrt{\frac{n}{d}})$-Tverberg partitions, and a point in the intersection of the convex hulls of the Tverberg parts. Our central idea is based on a lifting trick of Sarkaria [\emph{Isr. J. Math.} 1991], together with sampling ideas from Sober\'on [\emph{Combinatorica}, 2019], which we use to get a randomized algorithm for the \emph{Colorful Carath\'eodory} problem, improving upon the $d^{\Theta(\log d)}$ run-time of Mulzer and Stein [SoCG, 2015]. Lastly, we also give applications of our improved bounds to several computational problems.

papers.title: From Persistent Cohomology to Maps into Arbitrary Eilenberg-MacLane Spaces
papers.abstract: In this paper, we address the construction of Eilenberg-MacLane coordinates (functions from datasets to Eilenberg-MacLane spaces $K(G,n)$) that encode nontrivial persistent cohomology classes in arbitrary dimensions $n$ and coefficient group $G$. The construction leverages the connecting homomorphism in the long exact sequence in \v{C}ech cohomology, from the short exact sequence of sheaves of continuous maps with values in $G$, $EG$ and $BG$. Crucially, the derivation is constructive: we give an explicit, recursive formula for preimages under the connecting homomorphism, which yields a constructive version of a classical cohomology vanishing theorem and, in turn, an algorithm for general Eilenberg-MacLane coordinates. We validate our approach through experiments on synthetic datasets, and present novel examples of $K(\mathbb{Z}/2, 2)$-coordinates not addressed in prior work.

papers.title: K-subareas partitioning subject to coinciding boundary segments of neighboring subareas
papers.abstract: A method for the problem of partitioning an area into K subareas subject to coinciding boundary segments of neighboring subareas is presented. The given area may be non-convex and may additionally include obstacle areas. The proposed hierarchical method involves three steps: repeated bisection splitting, merging and the solution of traveling salesman problems. Geographic real-world outdoors areas data is used for the evaluation of the method. The benefit of computational simplicity at the cost of imbalanced subarea sizes is highlighted.
